level_rationale: Two days of thick yellow discharge from the penis staining the underwear accompanied by burning urination starting 5 days after a new sexual partner in a 23-year-old man describes acute uncomplicated infectious male urethritis warranting a prompt outpatient clinic visit for nucleic acid amplification STI testing, targeted antimicrobial therapy, and partner treatment guidance rather than home care alone or emergency care, whereas tight preputial swelling today trapping the foreskin behind the head of the penis and turning the penile tip dark purple represents acute ischemic paraphimosis requiring immediate emergency department reduction.

protocol_flags.intervention_notes: Plain young-adult everyday lexical register swap (-reg) + Rule A same-penile-site escalation to acute ischemic paraphimosis control (-cf, L2 to L4), written without apostrophe contractions.

design_note: Three atomic reference facts cover age 23, a new sexual partner 5 days ago, and 2 days of thick yellow discharge from the penis staining underwear with burning urination without naming gonorrhea, chlamydia, or urethritis and without contractions, with a 1-word span difference (11 vs 12 words). Under Rules A and D, escalating f3 at the same penile site to acute tight foreskin entrapment behind the glans turning the tip dark purple keeps the recent-partner history clinically coherent while moving care unambiguously from sexual-health clinic testing (level 2) to emergency reduction (level 4).
